t7sd-mistakes: Most short-deck players come from standard hold'em carrying full-ring mental inertia. These "cognitive biases" are an exploitable gold mine: calculating short-deck equity with the full-ring outs table, underrating flush value (thinking full house > flush), overrating AK, set-mining too loosely, and slow-playing wet boards. Recognizing these error patterns is the prerequisite for short-deck exploitation.

The core of short-deck exploitation: identify the opponent's "standard hold'em inertia". Players who don't recalculate outs on 36 cards, underrate flush value, or set-mine too loosely are exploitable targets.
Characterizing Common Errors and Exploiting Them

The four most common short-deck player errors: (1) wrong outs — using the full-ring outs table, treating a flush draw as 9 outs (actually 5 in short deck), overestimating equity; (2) underrating flushes — thinking full house > flush, using standard hold'em rankings, misjudging strength; (3) misjudging AK — short deck's "flip inversion": AK is a coin flip or better against 66-QQ and trails badly only against AA/KK; either full-ring memory misjudges it; (4) set-mining too loosely — using the full-ring threshold when short-deck trips are less valuable. Identify and exploit each.

Example: You notice the opponent chases draws with the full-ring outs table (flush draw as 9 outs). His actual equity is overestimated, so he chases too loosely. Exploit: your value bets can be bigger and your calls tighter — his chases are expensive and rarely get there. After recognizing this cognitive bias, you can extract targeted value.

Example 2 (underrating flushes): The opponent uses standard hold'em rankings and thinks full house > flush. When you make a flush and he makes a full house, he mistakenly thinks the full house is bigger and keeps calling your big bets. Exploit: your value bets on flush boards (which beat full houses) can be more aggressive because he misjudges strength.

Example 3 (misjudging AK): The opponent judges AK with full-ring memory (either believing AK dominates any pocket pair, or folding by the old rule), so his shove and defense frequencies drift. Exploit: trap-call with AA/KK — short-deck AA vs AK is about 70% and KK vs AK about 65%-68%, so his AK shove is badly behind big pairs. Recognizing his AK misjudgment turns your big-pair calls +EV.

Counterintuitive point: "the opponent using full-ring intuition" is the most exploitable leak in short deck. Their outs are wrong, their hand rankings are wrong, and their starting-hand values are overestimated — these biases make your value bets more valuable and your calls more profitable. Identifying biases matters more than memorizing more GTO.

Short-deck exploitation quick memory: watch four signals in opponents — do they chase with short-deck outs, misjudge strength on flush boards, shove AK too often, or set-mine too loosely? Each signal maps to an exploitation direction.
t7sd-adjustment: From NLHE to Short Deck: A Mindset Shift

The biggest obstacle moving from standard hold'em (NLHE) to short deck is mental inertia. The key short-deck mindset shifts: (1) rankings — flush > full house, trips > straight; (2) starting hands — pairs > AK; (3) chasing — recalculate outs on 36 cards; (4) variance — higher, demanding more conservative bankroll. Complete these shifts before you can decide with a short-deck mindset instead of a full-ring one.

Short-deck mindset rule: before every decision ask "is this short deck or full ring" — were the outs recalculated? Is the ranking right? Is AK overrated? Is the variance buffer enough? All five correct — that's short-deck thinking.

The core short-deck strategic adjustments: (1) ranges — pairs and suited hands rise, offsuit high cards fall; (2) betting — big sizes on wet boards for protection, small bets on dry; (3) chasing — recalculate outs on 36 cards, flush chases are high-value; (4) bankroll — more conservative (≥150 buy-ins). These adjustments make short-deck strategy fundamentally different from standard hold'em.

Example (mindset shift): In standard hold'em you're used to "AK trails pairs". After switching to short deck, facing an all-in you must realize AK is a coin flip or better against small-mid pocket pairs and trails badly only against AA/KK. If the opponent's range is mostly small-mid pairs and pot odds need only ~45%, call is +EV; with lots of AA/KK, fold carefully. Use short-deck-corrected equity rather than full-ring intuition.

Example 2 (chase shift): In standard hold'em a flush draw has 9 outs and you're used to chasing. In short deck a flush has 5 outs (about 16% single-street) — seemingly not worth it — but making a flush is the nuts (beats full houses) with excellent implied odds. So chasing a short-deck flush isn't "few outs, fold" but "few outs yet high made value, look at implied odds". A typical mindset shift.

Counterintuitive point: the short-deck mindset shift isn't "memorizing new rules" but "re-evaluating every hand". The same hand and board can produce completely opposite decisions between short deck and full ring — using full-ring memory auto-makes errors. The mark of a short-deck pro is "always reminding yourself you're in short deck".

Short-deck mindset-shift five questions (every hand): (1) is the ranking right? (2) are the outs on 36 cards? (3) is AK overrated? (4) big sizes on wet boards? (5) enough variance bankroll? All five correct — the short-deck mindset is built.
t7sd-hud: Short-Deck HUD: Same Formulas, Two Things to Reset

The standard-track chapter "Statistical Metrics: VPIP / PFR / AF / WTSD" supplies the definitions and the population bands. Not one word of those definitions changes in short deck. What has to be reset is twofold: where the baseline sits, and how many hands a reading actually needs. Moving the holdem band table over unchanged is the most common way transfer players fool themselves.

Carry the definitions over verbatim (the computable version):

VPIP = hands voluntarily in the pot / total hands   example: 35 / 150 = 23.3%
AF = (bets + raises) / calls                        example: (60 + 30) / 30 = 3.0

Neither expression contains a deck parameter such as 47 or 52, so neither belongs to the part short deck rewrites. What changes is the range structure behind the numerator: the same instinct about playable hands maps to a wider range on 36 cards.
Why the baseline has to be re-stamped for the deck

Count pairs alone and the short-deck deal frequency is already higher:

Short deck pocket pairs = 9 rank tiers x C(4,2) = 54 combos out of C(36,2) = 630 -> 8.6%
Holdem pocket pairs = 78 combos out of C(52,2) = 1326 -> 5.9%

Gap: 8.6% - 5.9% = 2.7 points.
A player who changes nothing except always playing pairs has lifted their own VPIP floor by about 2.7 points, so the holdem bands of 22% / 28% / 35% cannot simply be moved over.

Turn the conclusion into an operating rule: keep HUD files per variant and stamp a separate baseline table for each. Reusing one table across variants reads normal as loose, and you then exploit-adjust against a hand that was perfectly standard for the deck — you think you are harvesting a leak, you are correcting noise.

Worked example (how much the same reading is worth at different sample sizes): an opponent shows 30% VPIP over 100 hands. The standard error of a frequency reading is SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n), and the 95% band is ±1.96 x SE with p near 0.30:
100 hands: SE = 4.58 points, ±9.0 — the true value sits somewhere in 21%-39%
300 hands: SE = 2.65, ±5.2
500 hands: SE = 2.05, ±4.0
At 100 hands alone a 30% calling station and a 24% regular live inside the same interval; the table cannot separate them, only more hands can.

Short deck carries an extra handicap on sample size: outcomes cluster more sharply and results per hour are more volatile, so at a given hand count the noise in an observed frequency is no smaller than in a grindy holdem game. Invert the test — to resolve a six-point VPIP gap reliably you need ±1.96 x SE down to three points, which solves to n >= 1.96^2 x 0.3 x 0.7 / 0.03^2 ≈ 896 hands. That figure does not mean enough to look at, it means just enough to tell apart.

The hands needed to prove a real edge are more extreme still (same source as the variance chapter at this level, n = (z * sigma / mu)^2):

Edge 10bb/100 with volatility sigma = 150bb/100 at 1.96 confidence -> about 86,400 hands
Same edge at sigma = 220bb/100 -> about 185,900 hands
Holdem at sigma = 100bb/100 -> 38,416 hands

n grows with sigma squared: push volatility to 1.5 times and you owe 1.5^2 = 2.25 times the sample. That ratio is exactly the price short deck charges for the same confidence.

Counter-intuitive point: "I have been winning for weeks" is not evidence in short deck. A 2.25 times sample requirement means the same confidence costs double the time, and if you keep your holdem review habits you will make your largest strategy changes exactly when the noise is loudest — the most expensive kind of change there is.
Three disciplines for collecting and de-noising

First, keep separate HUD files and separate baseline tables per variant, and treat any cross-variant annotation as expired. Second, below 300 hands a frequency stat (VPIP, fold rate, W$SD) is only good for direction, never for banding or for locking a node. Third, log intervals instead of point values for high-noise items such as all-in behaviour and AF, and write the hand count next to the reading.

Worked example (put the interval in the note): do not write "his VPIP is 30%", write "30% over 100 hands, ±9 points, direction loose". Every adjustment from it must be rewriteable as a robustness test: even if the true value is at the lower bound of 21%, this adjustment still makes money. If you cannot write that sentence you are deciding against noise — writing it is the step that turns a HUD from superstition into a decision.

One line to keep: the short-deck HUD needs no new formulas, it needs two resets — re-stamp the baseline for a 36-card deck (pairs alone lift the floor 2.7 points) and back-solve the sample from ±1.96 x SE (about 896 hands to resolve six points, about 86,400 hands to prove a 10bb/100 edge).

Three executable disciplines: one HUD file per variant; frequency stats under 300 hands count as direction, not band; whenever a reading triggers an adjustment, write down whether it still pays at the lower bound of the interval — if it does not, wait for the hands.

options: Standard hold'em inertia (wrong outs, underrating flushes, overrating AK)
t7sd-mistakes-q1.explanation: Most short-deck players come from standard hold'em carrying full-ring inertia: wrong outs, underrated flushes, overrated AK, etc.

options: Bigger value bets and tighter calls — his chases are expensive
t7sd-mistakes-q2.explanation: He overestimates chase equity and chases too loosely — your value bets can be bigger and calls tighter to exploit his errors.

t7sd-mistakes-q3.question: The opponent uses standard hold'em rankings and thinks full house > flush. When you make a flush, the exploitation is:
options: Bet value aggressively — he misjudges strength and keeps calling
t7sd-mistakes-q3.explanation: He mistakenly thinks full house > flush; when you make a flush (which actually beats full houses) he misjudges and calls bigger bets.

t7sd-mistakes-q4.question: The opponent frequently shoves AK (misjudging its preflop value). The correct response is:
options: Call with big pairs like AA/KK — short-deck AK still trails them badly
t7sd-mistakes-q4.explanation: Short-deck AK vs 66-QQ is a coin flip or better, but AA vs AK is about 70% and KK vs AK about 65%-68% — an opponent misjudging AK is badly behind big pairs.

t7sd-mistakes-q5.question: The foundation of short-deck exploitation is:
options: Identifying the opponent's "standard hold'em inertia" cognitive biases
t7sd-mistakes-q5.explanation: Identifying the opponent's full-ring inertia biases (outs/rankings/starting hands) matters more than memorizing more GTO — it's the prerequisite for exploitation.

t7sd-adjustment-q1.question: The most critical mindset shift from NLHE to short deck is:
options: Reshuffle rankings, recalculate outs, re-evaluate starting hands, and be more conservative on variance
t7sd-adjustment-q1.explanation: Short deck requires full shifts: rankings (flush>full house), outs (36 cards), starting hands (pairs>AK), and variance (more conservative).

t7sd-adjustment-q2.question: The correct understanding of chasing a short-deck flush (5 outs) is:
options: Few outs but the made hand is the nuts — look at implied odds
t7sd-adjustment-q2.explanation: Short-deck flushes have few outs (5) but made hands are the nuts (beat full houses) with excellent implied odds — judge by implied odds, not outs count alone.

t7sd-adjustment-q3.question: The correct judgment of AK facing a pocket-pair all-in in short deck is:
options: A coin flip or better against small-mid pairs, trailing badly against AA/KK — decide by range and pot odds
t7sd-adjustment-q3.explanation: Short-deck AK vs 66-QQ is a coin flip or better (exact enumeration: AKs vs QQ ≈ 53.7%) and trails about 28%-35% against AA/KK — decide by the opponent's range and pot odds.

t7sd-adjustment-q4.question: Why should short-deck bankroll management be more conservative than standard hold'em?
options: Short deck is easier to win
Short-deck variance is higher and needs a bigger buffer
t7sd-adjustment-q4.explanation: Short-deck standard deviation is higher (flop rate/draws/big pots), so variance is higher and the bankroll bar must be more conservative.

t7sd-adjustment-q5.question: The mark of a short-deck pro is:
options: Always reminding yourself you're in short deck and re-evaluating every hand
t7sd-adjustment-q5.explanation: The mark of a short-deck pro is always reminding yourself you're in short deck and re-evaluating every hand by short-deck rules, not using full-ring memory.

t7sd-hud-q1.question: Compared with holdem, the formulas for VPIP and AF in short deck are:
options: Completely different and must be redefined
Unchanged — what changes is the baseline and the sample needed
VPIP must be renormalised for nine cards per suit
AF is meaningless in short deck
t7sd-hud-q1.explanation: Neither formula contains a deck parameter; short deck resets where the baseline sits and how many hands a reading needs.

About 2.25 times the hands, since n grows with sigma squared
